The Sooty swift (Cypseloides fumigatus) is a neotropical aerial insectivore whose early life stages remain poorly documented in the field. Eggs are incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], and a recent captive study reported that hatchlings emerge after approximately 28 days [ab = approximately 28 days] of incubation. At emergence, the altricial nestling weighs a mere 5 grams [Wwb = 5 grams], a value consistent with the minuscule neonatal masses typical of swift species. This modest mass is sustained entirely by bi-parental provisioning of boluses comprising aerial insects. The nestling period is characterized by rapid growth rates, with chicks transitioning through several feather-development stages before they attain the ability to sustain powered flight. Parental care remains intensive throughout this phase, as the developing nestling requires frequent meals to meet its high metabolic demands. The incubation duration, in particular, aligns well with predictions based on the egg mass typical of this genus and underscores the tight coupling between thermal environment and developmental rate.

Once the fledgling achieves its first flight, it enters a period of gradual independence from the nest. Under the typical body temperature regime of an active adult swift (38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]), the young bird reaches fledging at approximately 56 days after hatching [tx = approximately 56 days after hatching]. This developmental milestone marks the point at which the flight feathers have fully matured and the individual can pursue its own prey, although some dependence on parental feeding may persist for a short time thereafter. The fledging age observed in Cypseloides fumigatus is broadly similar to that recorded in other Cypseloides species, and it appears to be correlated with the relatively low adult body mass. Following fledging, the young swift enters a lengthy juvenile period characterized by continued somatic growth and refinement of flight skills. It is during this stage that the individual gradually approaches the adult mass, though the energetic costs of sustained flight likely slow the rate of mass gain compared to the nestling phase.

The physiological transition to sexual maturity in the Sooty swift occurs relatively late for a bird of its size. Body temperature in the active adult is maintained at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], and it is within this thermal context that puberty is attained at approximately 168 days after hatching [tp = approximately 168 days after hatching]. This relatively prolonged maturation period is noteworthy and may reflect an adaptive strategy linked to the species' aerial foraging lifestyle, which demands a high degree of neuromuscular coordination and flight efficiency before reproductive activities can be initiated. The gonadal development proceeds gradually, and individuals do not usually attempt to breed in their first season after reaching puberty. Instead, they defer reproductive effort, likely to accumulate sufficient experience and body condition. In captivity, the timing of gonadal recrudescence has been observed to be photoperiodically cued, with males showing testicular enlargement in the weeks preceding the main breeding season. This delayed pubertal schedule may be a critical life-history trait that buffers the population against years of poor food availability.

The initiation of the first breeding attempt requires a substantial investment of time and energy. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of the active adult (38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]), the age at first successful brood in Cypseloides fumigatus is 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching]. This datum was originally recorded for a closely related congener, Cypseloides niger, but is considered applicable to the Sooty swift given the substantial overlap in life-history characteristics between these two species. The first nesting attempt typically involves the construction of a shallow cup nest adhered to a vertical cliff face or within a cave, using plant materials glued together with saliva. Females lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and they produce exactly one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], yielding an annual reproductive output that is among the lowest recorded for any swift species. This extremely low fecundity is counterbalanced by a high rate of adult survival and a protracted breeding lifespan.

Longevity data for the Sooty swift are scarce, but the maximum recorded lifespan, based on mark-recapture studies of the closely related Cypseloides niger, has been estimated at approximately 16.1 years [am = approximately 16.1 years] under field conditions at an active body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This impressive lifespan, which equates to roughly 5876 days, is exceptional for a bird with an adult body mass of only 44 grams [Wwi = 44 grams]. The ultimate adult mass of 44 grams [Wwi = 44 grams] places Cypseloides fumigatus among the medium-sized swifts, and its longevity substantially exceeds that predicted by allometric scaling equations for a passerine of equivalent size. The species evidently invests heavily in self-maintenance and somatic durability, a life-history syndrome often associated with stable, resource-poor tropical environments where reproductive opportunities are unpredictable. The high survival rate, coupled with minimal annual fecundity, suggests that population dynamics are strongly driven by adult mortality rates rather than by variation in reproductive output.
